clinicalPearls: A myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap neoplasm with leucocytosis and prominent granulocytic dysplasia
It is, by definition, negative for the BCR-ABL1 fusion, distinguishing it from classic chronic myeloid leukaemia
The blood shows neutrophilia with dysgranulopoiesis and immature granulocyte precursors, but minimal basophilia
Monocytosis is not prominent, which helps separate it from chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia
SETBP1 and ASXL1 mutations are recurrent and associated with a poorer outcome
It generally carries a worse prognosis than classic chronic myeloid leukaemia and lacks a specifically targeted therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Atypical chronic myeloid leukaemia is a clonal stem cell neoplasm combining dysplastic and proliferative features. It lacks the BCR-ABL1 fusion that defines classic chronic myeloid leukaemia, and instead is associated with mutations such as SETBP1 and ASXL1 that promote clonal granulocyte proliferation with abnormal (dysplastic) maturation. The dysgranulopoiesis produces functionally abnormal neutrophils and their precursors in the blood, while ineffective haematopoiesis can cause cytopenias, and the disease has a substantial risk of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film demonstrating dysgranulopoiesis
Exclusion of reactive and other myeloid neoplasms
redFlags: Progressive cytopenias with bleeding or infection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor with short median survival in many series and a significant risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia; allogeneic transplantation is the main potentially curative option.
pitfalls: Assuming chronic myeloid leukaemia without confirming BCR-ABL1 status
Confusing it with chronic neutrophilic leukaemia or CMML
Overlooking prognostic mutations that inform transplant decisions
management: Recognise that tyrosine kinase inhibitors are ineffective because the disease is BCR-ABL1 negative, and control the leucocytosis with cytoreductive therapy such as hydroxycarbamide
Consider hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine, and ruxolitinib in selected cases, for disease control
Refer eligible patients for allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only potentially curative option
Provide supportive care with transfusion for symptomatic cytopenias, growth factor support and prompt treatment of infection
Monitor closely for transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia
Manage through a specialist haematology multidisciplinary team with early transplant referral
